entries.title: Canada's Carney welcomes associate status idea in EU speech
entries.summary: Mark Carney wants to strengthen Canada's ties to the European Union amid a growing rift with the US under Donald Trump. The US president has threatened to halt trade with Europe if it makes Canada an associate EU member.
entries.content:
September 17, 2026

Mark Carney wants to strengthen Canada's ties to the European Union amid a growing rift with the US under Donald Trump. The US president has threatened to halt trade with Europe if it makes Canada an associate EU member.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was addressing the European Parliament on Thursday, in a speech that focused on Canada's and the European Union's shared security and economic interests.

In an address in which Carney spoke in English, French and German, the Canadian prime minister lauded European culture and values of democracy, freedom and human rights, which he said Canada shares.

"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," the Canadian leader told the chamber, to applause.

Europe and Canada are 'stronger together', Carney tells EU Parliament

"We hold common values for which we have always fought and in whose defense we must always remain vigilant," he said.

Carney also said his country "welcomes" the "ambition" of the EU's proposal of an "associated membership".

"Europe and Canada are each strong," he said. But he added that "Europe and Canada are even stronger together."

"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners,” he said. "We do not seek power to dominate others."

"The ​objective is not ⁠self-sufficiency, ​it's ​collective resilience", Carney ​said.

His speech to European lawmakers comes as the EU and Canada look to strengthen their ties amid a growing rift between Canada and its southern neighbor and main trading partner, the US.

Ties between Canada and the US have hit a historic low in recent months, with the North American neighbors locked in an escalating trade war since Carney and US President Donald Trump failed to agree on a deal this summer. 

EU defends Canada alliance plan after Trump tariffs threat

On Wednesday, the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was willing to make Canada its first-ever "associate member," days after the Wall Street Journal reported that Carney was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc, a position that does not currently exist.

During her State of the EU address, von der Leyen said the bloc needed to adapt to an "openly hostile world" marked by aggressive power politics and "frayed relationships," the latter a clear nod to the turbulent ties between Brussels and Washington since Trump returned to the White House.

Prior to his visit this week, Carney had confirmed that he wanted to establish a "unique alliance" between Canada and the EU.

"We share the same values, we have the same priorities and ​we have very complementary strengths," the prime minister said.

Trump on Wednesday slammed the EU's plans to make Canada an associate member. 

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina. The US president also described the prospect of Canada joining the EU as "laughable."

How did the US-Canada relationship come to this?

Ties between Canada and the US have plummeted since Trump began his second term in January 2025. He has targeted Canada with tariffs and suggested that the US could annex Canada as its 51st state. 

Trump has also referred to Carney, as well as his predecessor as prime minister, Justin Trudeau, as the "governor" of Canada.

The growing rift has also seen Trump sign an executive order renaming Lake Ontario, a Great Lake between the US and Canada, to "Lake America."

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Jews once lived lived here: When houses tell stories
entries.summary: Time and again, residents tracing the history of their homes discover the lives of Jewish predecessors who fled or were deported amid stories of suffering and loss.
entries.content:
September 17, 2026

Time and again, residents tracing the history of their homes discover the lives of Jewish predecessors who fled or were deported amid stories of suffering and loss.

Over the years, many people have passed through this fourth-floor apartment in an old Berlin building. Here, at Rosenheimer Straße 40, they have sat on the sofa and gathered around the kitchen table. They have looked out the window and let their minds wander.

Marie Rolshoven has lived here with her family since 2007. "The feeling of crossing that threshold, the same one the former residents crossed for the last time, stays with you," she says. She knows that Jews once lived here, and none of them survived the Nazi era.

Driven from their homes

After the National Socialists seized power in January 1933, it quickly became clear that Jews were considered second-class citizens under Nazi rule. Even the right to remain in their homes could no longer be taken for granted.

"A racially conscious fellow citizen cannot be expected to share a household with a Jew," the Nazi party newspaper Völkischer Beobachter wrote on September 18, 1938, claiming that landlords were therefore entitled to terminate leases without notice. On April 30, 1939, the law took effect. Jewish tenants and property owners were forced to leave their homes and move into buildings designated by the authorities, referred to in Nazi jargon as "Judenhäuser"(Jewish houses).

Several people were forcibly housed in Henny and Carl Möller's apartment at Rosenheimer Straße 40. In the end, there were nine of them. In the fall of 1941, Nazi authorities began systematically deporting Jews to ghettos and camps in Eastern Europe.

Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels wrote in his diary: "The main thing is that the capital of the Reich be cleansed of Jews; and I will neither rest nor relent until this goal is fully achieved." The residents of Rosenheimer Straße were among those who were subsequently deported.

Remembering at the original site

Marie Rolshoven aims to honor the fate of these individuals. In 2016, she, along with her late mother and a friend, founded the initiative Denk Mal Am Ort (a wordplay meaning both "Think about it at the site" and "Memorial at the Site") inspired by the Amsterdam project Open Jewish Homes.

The idea is to invite people to the very location where everyday life once occurred. "You feel a strong connection to these individuals through the actual site," says Rolshoven. "It's different from visiting a memorial."

'My brother's bed used to be right here'

Two floors below, her neighbors had a similar experience. Denk Mal Am Ort found out that the Jewish Katzenellenbogen family had previously rented the apartment.

The family escaped Nazi Germany in 1939, just in time. "In 2018, 92-year-old Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen was invited back here, accompanied by his daughter, son-in-law, and grandson,” Rolshoven tells DW.

The Denk Mal Am Ort initiative discovered him through Facebook. Rolshoven recounts how touched the visitors were when the former resident walked in and remarked, "Yes, I remember it clearly. My brother's bed used to be right here. He was 10 when we had to leave the country."

Soon there will be no eyewitnesses left

Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen has since passed away, along with many other eyewitnesses. This highlights the importance of intergenerational remembrance, according to Rolshoven. She has already welcomed a descendant of a former resident into her home.

Claudia Samter's mother managed to escape from Berlin to Argentina, but her aunt was not as fortunate. Seeking assistance in tracing her family's history, Claudia contacted Denk Mal Am Ort. It turned out that her aunt had once been housed in Rolshoven's apartment.

Claudia Samter has already visited twice. "After all, there's no grave in a cemetery for her to visit," says Rolshoven. "We sat at the kitchen table to talk about life today and tomorrow, and we laughed a lot and cried, too. It felt good to give this space a new purpose once again."

Denk Mal Am Ort has so far organized 90 commemorative events in eight cities this year. Many young descendants attended, according to Rolshoven. "Knowing that they had stood in this stairwell and touched the same doorknob helped them."

Seeking traces of ancestors

19-year-old Adam Ethan Klein from Switzerland also wanted to learn more about his ancestors' history. "I always knew there was a story of escape, but it was never a significant topic at home,” he says.

"They'd say, ‘Yes, your great-grandparents left Germany in 1938, just in time. Luckily, otherwise you wouldn't be here today'."

Klein says his decision to dig deeper was prompted by the spread ofantisemitism, as well as the widespread slogan "Never again is now." (Editor's note: This slogan serves as a call to actively confront antisemitism, hatred, and threats to democracy today.)

The whole family was aware of a suitcase belonging to his maternal great-grandfather in the attic. However, no one ever looked inside until Adam finally opened the suitcase and discovered dozens of documents. He also found a letter from the Hanover District Court dated June 12, 1933, addressed to his great-grandfather, attorney Max Haas.

The letter stated: "As of today, following the decree issued by the Minister of Justice, you have been removed from the list of licensed attorneys."

'They were above all one thing: Jews'

Klein was profoundly affected by the letter: "With this single sentence, it became unmistakably clear to the families that they were not quite what they had aspired to be for generations: an average German family. From that moment on, they were above all one thing: Jews."

For Klein, this was a troubling realization. So was the news that someone had stabbed an ultra-Orthodox Jew to death in Zurich while shouting antisemitic slogans. The attack occurred not far from the synagogue where he had shortly before celebrated a cousin's bar mitzvah. (Editor's note: In Judaism, a bar mitzvah is a ceremony that marks a young person's coming of age in religious matters.)

"For the first time in my life, I felt that unsettling sensation of not quite belonging. Yet Zurich is my home, the city where I've lived carefree as a Jewish Swiss from birth," Adam would later write.

"That was definitely new, uncharted territory for me. I had always thought that such things don't happen in Switzerland. Maybe that was a bit naive of me," he admits.

The subject would not let him go. Adam continued his research, determined to write his high school graduation thesis about his relatives. In the spring of 2024, he set off with his parents, sister, grandmother, uncles, aunts and several cousins to visit the places where their ancestors had lived.

A magical encounter

At some point during their journey, they found themselves in Stuttgart, standing in front of a five-story building at Hölderlinstraße 55, when a man on a bike emerged from the courtyard and approached them.

"So, are you taking a guided tour of the city, or are you planning to move here?" he asked jokingly. The man was Thomas Koch, who had spent time researching the former residents of his house. When he heard the answer, "No, we're just checking out where our ancestors lived," he was thrilled.

Koch had already discovered that the former owners of the house, the Merzbacher brothers, sold it in 1936 for 75,000 Reichsmarks. From that amount, they had to pay 70,000 Reichsmarks in wealth taxes and the Reich Emigration Tax. The remaining sum was just enough to cover the ship fares to Brazil and the United States.

From 1937 to 1938, a family named Hirschheimer, who worked in the plywood trade, lived on the ground floor before they were forcibly relocated to a "Judenhaus." Their trail went cold in 1939, as Koch found no further records. So, he asked, "Are you the Hirschheimer family?" They were indeed.

Koch describes the encounter as magical. Adolf and Auguste Hirschheimer were Adam's great-great-grandparents, and their daughter, Ilse, was married to Max Haas.

Adam Klein and Thomas Koch have kept in touch since then. The next time Adam visited Stuttgart, he was invited over for coffee and cake.

Adam was impressed by the beautiful apartment. "It was fascinating to imagine how my ancestors once lived there, and it probably wasn't that different. Back then, there was likely coffee and cake as well."

Adam showed Koch photos of his grandmother, Ilse, who had married at the synagogue in Stuttgart, standing in the living room in her wedding gown. "In front of the door that we still have," says Koch.

“It was really moving to discover new roommates in a historical context set in the past. And I think this experience — this process of putting myself in their shoes — is a deeply empathetic one that simply brings us together through this apartment.”

Shattered identities

Ilse and Max Haas found refuge in England, while the Hirschheimers emigrated to Switzerland in 1939. Adolf Hirschheimer died in 1940 from a heart condition, but Adam, his great-great-grandson, believes he "certainly also died of a broken heart."

Auguste was brought to England by her son-in-law, Max, where the family felt homesick. "There, we were the Jews; here, we are the Germans. Try figuring that out," Ilse Haas wrote to a friend. Adam chose these lines as the title for his thesis.

Adam's great-grandparents could not find peace after being stripped of their homeland. From England, they eventually went to Israel and, at some point, returned to Europe — to Switzerland.

"At the end of their lives, my great-grandparents settled just a two-hour drive from their old homeland," Adam wrote. "When I look at their lives through the eyes of a great-grandson, it becomes clear that after breaking ties with Germany, they never managed to put down roots anywhere again."

"Remembering is important because, ultimately, we have to learn from history," says Adam. "And I think every single person has a responsibility— and the power — to actively keep memories alive. And hopefully, that can happen even without eyewitnesses.” For example, in his ancestors' former apartment.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Fiji declares HIV a national crisis, 1 in 60 adults carry it
entries.summary: Fiji's government estimates that HIV prevalence has almost tripled in the last five years. It's expanding testing, prevention and treatment services. In 2025 the tiny island recorded 16 times more new cases than in 2019.
entries.content:
HealthFiji

Fiji declares HIV a national crisis, 1 in 60 adults carry it

September 17, 2026

Fiji's government estimates that HIV prevalence has almost tripled in the last five years. It's expanding testing, prevention and treatment services. In 2025 the tiny island recorded 16 times more new cases than in 2019.

Fiji has declared HIV a national health crisis, pledging a "whole-of-government response to address the significant rise in HIV cases and protect communities across the country." 

The Pacific island's government announced the move earlier this week, saying it had recorded 2,016 new HIV diagnoses in 2025 — 16 times the number recorded in 2019. The figures point to the virus spreading beyond high-risk groups like drug users and sex workers into the wider population.

Fiji said the known adult prevalence of the virus had almost tripled in five years in the country of a little more than 900,000 people.

What did Fiji's government say about HIV and its response?

"An estimated one in every 60 adults is now living with HIV, compared with one in 167 five years ago," the government said.

"Among pregnant women, two in every 100 are living with HIV, while 59 babies were born with HIV in 2025, with 18 dying before their first birthday," it warned.

However, the government also said that expanded testing was helping health services reach more people and identify cases that might have previously gone undetected, noting a period of slower surveillance starting around a decade ago.

Health Minister Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu and four other revlevant Cabinet ministers would form a sub-committe to "help remove barriers to rapid action."

The administration based in the capital and port city Suva said it was expanding access to free HIV testing, prevention services and treatment — including rapid testing, prevention medecine for people at high risk, harm-reduction measures for people who inject drugs and free treatment for diagnosed HIV sufferers.

"The response is focused on protecting lives, improving access to health services and reducing stigma," the government said. "Fiji is also receiving support from international partners, including Australia, New Zealand, India, the Global Fund and the United Nations."

It reminded people that testing was free and confidential across the country, saying "knowing your HIV status allows you to take informed steps to protect your health and others."

UNAIDS welcomes response, estimates less than half of Fiji's HIV sufferers know their status

UNAIDS in Geneva responded to the move on Wednesday, welcoming Fiji's decision to accelerate its response.

"Fiji has recognized the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response," said UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima. "It is also a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over. HIV epidemics can change quickly, and countries need health and community systems that are ready to respond urgently."

The UN organization said that among Fijian cases with a known mode of transmission, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42% to injecting drug use.

UNAIDS estimated that new infections increased 12-fold between 2010 and 2025 in Fiji. It also said that of an estimated 9,100 people living with the virus in 2025, "only 39% knew their HIV status and just 22% were accessing antiretroviral treatment."

However, giving medical advances in recent years and increased efficacy of treatments, it said that there was time to turn the tide.

"The national crisis declaration is a call for action, not fear. HIV is not transmitted through everyday contact, and people on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load do not sexually transmit HIV," said UNAIDS' Eamonn Murphy. "Fiji still has an opportunity to change the course of this epidemic."

The country director for Fiji at UNAIDS, Renata Ram, told the AFP news agency that transmission rates started rising around 2019 when a group of "very high-risk" injecting drug users emerged, primarily in the sex worker community.

Pacific islands like Fiji have become transit hubs for drugs from Latin America and Asia destined for the lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand. This has also led to increased drug use on the islands themselves, often as a result of foreign crime syndicates paying their local associates with product.

entries.title: Australia to restrict student, backpacker visas in migration clampdown
entries.summary: The Australian interior minister said reducing migration is needed to address housing pressures. The move comes amid a far-right surge in the polls.
entries.content:
Australia

Australia to cut student, backpacker visas in migration curb

September 17, 2026

The Australian interior minister said reducing migration is needed to address housing pressures. The move comes amid a far-right surge in the polls.

Australia will cut migration by toughening visa rules for foreign students, backpackers, and working holiday-makers, the Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Thursday.

Under the new rules, foreign students will no longer be allowed to bring partners and children to join them while they study in Australia, while people who overstay their working holiday visas will face tougher enforcement.

The government is also cracking down on so-called "visa hopping," where foreign migrants who are already in Australia move from one type of temporary visa to another to extend their stay.

"If you want to come on a temporary basis to Australia, apply for a temporary visa. If you want ‌to ​come to Australia permanently, apply for a permanent visa. And if you no longer have a valid visa, you should leave Australia," Burke said.

What else did the Home Affairs Minister say about the migration reforms?

In remarks to the National Press Club in Canberra on Thursday, Burke insisted that immigration remains "fundamentally a strength" for Australia, but acknowledged that rules needed adjusting to ease pressure on housing.

"We need immigration to soften enough that housing has a chance to catch up," he said, while stressing the housing shortage was not caused by migrants.

Burke said it was "simply demonstrably wrong" that his ruling center-left Labor party was beefing up its visa rules as a response to a surge in the polls by the far-right One Nation.

This year, the group has become one of the country's most popular parties, campaigning on pledges to slash migration to the country as part of its "Australia First" approach, which has drawn similarities to US President Donald Trump.

The hard-right party said this week that it would cut the number of temporary migrants by 750,000 over the next three years to give Australians "breathing space."

The cost of living and immigration have ranked as some of voters' most pressing concerns in recent polls.

What is the migration situation in Australia?

The changes are set to see net annual migration fall from the current 300,000 to around 225,000 by 2028. That would see numbers return to the levels before the Covid-19 pandemic.

Annual migration surged to its highest level of 538,000 in 2022, after borders reopened.

Data on Thursday showed that migration numbers had declined to 292,100 in the year to March, 47% below the peak following the pandemic, Burke said.

Students make up the biggest immigrant group: some 753,000 foreign students live in Australia, most of whom come from China and India.

The reforms will see Australia return to its policy of a decade earlier when those who overstayed were given two weeks to leave the country or face detention and deportation, the minister said.

People seeking to extend their working holiday visas in rural areas will enter a ballot for a second or third year.

Applicants with skills in construction and housing will be prioritized for visas, Burke said.

Relatives of visa holders wanting to visit the country will have "no further stay" conditions applied to their visas.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.summary: A cafe and kiosk were damaged overnight in Frankfurt, in what police said are the latest in a series of mysterious blasts in the area. Meanwhile, diesel prices in Germany have hit an all-time high. More on DW.
entries.content:
Published September 17, 2026last updated September 17, 2026

A cafe and kiosk were damaged overnight in Frankfurt, in what police said are the latest in a series of mysterious blasts in the area. Meanwhile, diesel prices in Germany have hit an all-time high. More on DW.

  • Diesel prices in Germany hit all-time high

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Thursday, September 17, 2026:

Skip next section Heat and drought set to wither Germany's 2026 potato harvest

Heat and drought set to wither Germany's 2026 potato harvest

Extreme heat and drought this summer will lead to a weak potato harvest in northwestern Europe this year, according to an analysis released on Thursday by the UK-based Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU).

In Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands, a combined shortage of 3,1 million tons compared to the five-year average harvest is expected.

The data shows the weak harvest will hit Germany particularly hard, with the country's share of the total expected potato harvest shortage coming in at 1,13 million tons.

These figures do not yet represent a final harvest report, but are an estimate.

"As fall begins, the effects of the record-breaking summer heat and drought on food and agriculture are becoming clear," said ECIU analyst Tom Lancaster.

Potatoes are among the crops in Europe that require the most water.

The analysis also reports a significant increase in prices. In Germany, spuds served at dinner are set to cost up to €280 per metric ton, compared to around €150 last year.

The expected 2026 harvest shortfall comes after oversupply in 2025 flooded the market. 

Skip next section Germany backs social media ban for under-13s

Germany backs social media ban for under-13s

Karin Prien,Germany's education minister, backed plans to restrict social media use among young people and children. "Any system will have to comply with data protection rules and minimize the amount of information that is collected about the user, without age-verification data being transmitted online. However, the primary responsibility for protecting minors lies with the social media platforms themselves," Prien told German public broadcaster ZDF on Thursday.

In addition to requesting age checks, Prien said media education and providing more information on the issue to parents are key. On Wednesday, the president of the European Commission,Ursula von der Leyen, proposed that children under the age of 13 be banned from accessing social media platforms such asTikTok, Snapchat, and Instagram. They would be able to use "mini-accounts" controlled and supervised by parents, with a maximum usage of one hour per day, and open a separate account from the age of 15.

Changes to social media platforms

Prien said the restrictions should be part of a broader, more comprehensive strategy. She also called for a rule under which children under the age of three have no screen time or access to digital services. The education minister announced plans as early as October for a German interim solution while rules are consolidated at the EU level. Under the EU proposals, social media platforms would be required to introduce safer designs, including measures to prevent endless scrolling and videos from playing automatically. The plans also include limits on screen time and other measures aimed at protecting young people.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: New Germany coach Jürgen Klopp introduces squad

IN DEPTH: New Germany coach Jürgen Klopp introduces squad

Kicking off his tenure as Germany's new head coach, Jürgen Klopp has named a huge squad of 44 players for his first four games, splitting them into two groups. A host of new faces is included.

Read the full story here.

Skip next section Authorities advice mosquito protection amid Malaria cases near Frankfurt Airport

Authorities advice mosquito protection amid Malaria cases near Frankfurt Airport

Health authorities in Frankfurt are advising residents to consider taking precautions against mosquitoes after several recent malaria cases in the region believed to have been caused by the insects having stowed away on aircraft.

This week, two people living in the vicinity of Frankfurt Airport were reported to have contracted malaria.

In August,  two Frankfurt Airport employees died after contracting malaria in an outbreak believed to have been caused by infected mosquitoes brought into Germany on an aircraft. Four other workers were infected, but recovered without complications.

The cases are part of a rare outbreak of so-called airport malaria, with the six employees infected despite not having traveled to a malaria-risk country. Authorities have not shared details about the two cases this week.

According to Germany's Robert Koch health institute, cases of airport malaria are extremely rare.

Data cited by DPA news agency shows that between 1969 and 2024, only 145 cases of locally contracted malaria were reported in Europe. At least 105 of those cases involved mosquitoes arriving on planes.

Most of these cases were in France, with only 9 reported in Germany in this time frame, making the 2026 outbreak a statistical outlier.

Malaria is native to tropical environments, and the vast majority of cases in Europe occur in summer.

Skip next section Merz to campaign in Berlin ahead of critical state election

Merz to campaign in Berlin ahead of critical state election

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will appear on Thursday at joint campaign event with lead Christian Democratic Union (CDU) candidate Stefan Evers, ahead of the Berlin House of Representatives election on Sunday.

Merz is facing pressure for the CDU to perform in Berlin after the CDU's state election drubbing earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt.

On Wednesday, all eight Christian Democratic Union (CDU) state premiers  publicly backed Merz amid growing unease over his leadership.

In Berlin, only a few percentage points separate the top four parties: the conservative CDU, the Left Party, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), and the environmentalist Greens.

The CDU's lead candidate, state finance minister Stefan Evers, has managed to keep the conservatives' chances afloat, with the party is polling around 20%, narrowly behind The Left and just ahead of the AfD.

A state election in nearby Mecklenburg- West Pomerania will also take place Sunday, with polling showing the CDU barely hanging on at around 7%, which is dangerously close to the 5% threshold needed to win seats in parliament.

Although the CDU has not traditionally performed well in the northeast German state, a 7% result at the polls would be the worst CDU election performance since World War II.

Skip next section Diesel prices in Germany hit record high

Diesel prices in Germany hit record high

Figures from the ADAC motoring organization released on Thursday show German diesel prices have surged to a new record, reaching an average price per liter of €2.45 ($2.81).

For US readers, that is equivalent to over $10.60 per gallon.

Since the Iran war started, fuel prices in Germany have surged. On Wednesday, the ADAC reported the price of ordinary gasoline at another record high of €2.314 ($2.65) per liter on average.

Measures to provide price relief in the spring expired in June, but German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday that the government would "react to price gouging." 

No new measures have yet been announced. Coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD), have called for a windfall tax on oil companies, an idea Merz has rejected.

Skip next section Mysterious explosions reported in Frankfurt

Mysterious explosions reported in Frankfurt

Residents in two Frankfurt neighborhoods were shaken from sleep early Thursday morning by mysterious explosions.

Police said explosives were set off shortly after 4 a.m. in front of a cafe in the city's "Nordend" neighborhood, and a few minutes later in front of a kiosk in the city center.

No injuries were reported. Images of the cafe showed a shattered glass facade and shards blown out onto the street.

"We have officers on the scene," a police spokeswoman told Germany's DPA news agency. "We're working hard on it," she added, referring to the ongoing investigation.

Police have not released any information about a motive or possible suspects.

In the past few days, there had been two explosions in Frankfurt and one in nearby Offenbach. Both caused minor damage and no injuries.

Early Monday morning, there was an explosion at an apartment building in Frankfurt-Bockenheim.

Early Sunday morning, there were also explosions in Frankfurt's Sachsenhausen district and in Offenbach. A bar, a cafe, and a newsstand were damaged in the incidents.

Following the explosion in Sachsenhausen, a 15-year-old suspect was arrested and is currently in pretrial detention.

This week's blasts come after repeated explosions in the Rhine-Main region over the past weeks and months.

Police have attributed several of these incidents to organized crime and the phenomenon of "violence as a service," in which teenagers and young adults are specifically recruited to carry out these acts, local public broadcaster HR reported.

Authorities have not said whether they consider Thursday morning's explosions to be one of these cases.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen from Bonn as we launch our coverage of what Germany is talking about today. 

Overnight in Frankfurt, two separate explosions caused minor damage to small businesses. Police have not released information on suspects or a possible motive.

And in Berlin, Chancellor Friedrich Merz will attend a conservative campaign event ahead of a critical state election on Sunday.

Skip next section India's Foreign Ministry slams reports that world leaders fell ill after BRICS summit

India's Foreign Ministry slams reports that world leaders fell ill after BRICS summit

India's Ministry of External Affairs has rejected social media claims that several world leaders fell ill after attending the BRICS Summit held in New Delhi on September 12-13, calling the reports "fake" and warning against "malicious" posts.

The MEA's fact-checking unit posted on X: "Fake Alert!!! 🚨🚨🚨 We caution against such malicious posts on social media platforms!" This included a social media post by Polymarket, one of the world's largest prediction market platforms.

The clarification followed genuine confirmation from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa's office that he had withdrawn from public engagements after returning from the summit, having been advised to rest due to ill health.

Separately, unverified posts claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping fainted and left the summit early for medical treatment. The claim originated from Wanjun Xie, chairman of the China Democracy Party, and was not confirmed by Chinese or Indian officials. Beijing has banned the party.

Xi is confirmed to have attended the summit and met bilaterally with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Skip next section India vows to protect trade and economic interests amid threat of US's Russia-linked tariffs

India vows to protect trade and economic interests amid threat of US's Russia-linked tariffs

India said Thursday it remains committed to securing energy supplies for its 1.4 billion people and will keep sourcing oil from diverse suppliers, hours after the US House of Representatives passed a bill authorizing tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas, including India, along with new sanctions tied to Russia's war in Ukraine.

The bill now goes to President Donald Trump for signature.

India's Ministry of External Affairs issued a statement responding directly to the legislation: "India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people. It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics."

The ministry said it had raised the issue with US officials in recent months, adding, "Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side."

"The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests," the statement added, saying it would work with trade and industry bodies on the legislation's implications.

India is the world's third-largest oil importer, and Russia has become one of its largest suppliers as well as a longstanding strategic and military partner. New Delhi has consistently defended the relationship as necessary for its energy needs, resisting outside pressure to scale it back.

What do we know about the sanctions?

The package targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, old tankers it uses to circumvent sanctions.

More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries that rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. Beijing and New Delhi are expected to be the main targets of such measures.

The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran.

To learn more about the bill passed by the US Congress, click here.

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again bringing you the latest from across India.

….And we start with the United States. The US Congress has passed its Russia sanctions bill, and the repercussions are being felt far and wide, including in India, where the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said the country will protect its trade and economic interests.

The MEA has also been busy debunking the narrative that several world leaders have fallen sick after their trip to India for the BRICS summit.

In other news, the Indian Supreme Court has dismissed an appeal by Prime Minister Modi's government to deny disability pension granted to veterans.

entries.title: Saint, sinner or feminist icon: How Mary Magdalene's image evolved through time
entries.summary: From "Apostle of the Apostles" to prostitute, Mary Magdalene has been assigned a wide variety of roles, as a new exhibition shows.
entries.content:
Europe

Saint, sinner or feminist icon: Mary Magdalene through time

September 17, 2026

From "Apostle of the Apostles" to prostitute, Mary Magdalene has been assigned a wide variety of roles, as a new exhibition shows.

Apostle, prostitute, penitent and confidante of Jesus — just a few of the roles assigned to Mary Magdalene since the early days of Christianity.

Artists from the Renaissance to the Baroque period, including Titian, El Greco and Georges de la Tour, depicted her in the 16th and 17th centuries as a repentant penitent; Rembrandt portrayed her as a witness to Christ's resurrection; and Max Beckmann, a representative of the New Objectivity movement, depicted her as a sinner in 1917.

Nearly a century later, she was portrayed by Lady Gaga in a music video.

"Mary Magdalene is probably the most multifaceted and enigmatic figure in the Bible, and also one of the most enigmatic in European cultural history," says Bastian Eclercy, curator of the exhibition "Mary Magdalene: Sin. Pray. Love" at the Städel Museum in Frankfurt. "She appears countless times in art history."

What do we know about Mary Magdalene?

Very little is known about Mary Magdalene from the Bible, yet she plays an important role in the New Testament.

The Gospels recount that Jesus delivered her from seven demons, and that she accompanied Jesus and witnessed his crucifixion and burial. On Easter morning, she discovered the empty tomb and became the first witness to the Resurrection. She then proclaimed the message of the risen Christ to Jesus' disciples: "She is then referred to as the Apostula Apostulorum, that is, the Apostle of the Apostles," explains Bastian Eclercy. "This gives her a very central role in the history of salvation."

But it didn't stop there.

Around 600 AD, Pope Gregory the Great permanently distorted the image of Mary Magdalene by merging her with two other women mentioned in the Bible: an unnamed woman, the "sinner" mentioned in the Gospel of Luke who washed Christ's feet, and Mary of Bethany (who also washed his feet). The Pope claimed that the seven demons cast out of Mary Magdalene by Jesus represented the seven deadly sins. His sermon played a decisive role in shaping Mary Magdalene's reputation as a repentant prostitute — something for which there is absolutely no evidence in the Bible.

Mary Magdalene's remains are in France — allegedly

In the High Middle Ages, a legend emerged to the effect that Mary Magdalene, together with Lazarus and a group of companions, had been cast adrift in a boat on the Mediterranean; with divine help, she is said to have reached the coast of Provence in France, where she first preached the Gospel and then lived in a cave for some 30 years, doing penance.

Even today, two French towns claim to hold her remains: Vezelay in Burgundy and Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume in Provence.

In the 16th century, finally, the Reformation and Renaissance humanism brought about a change in thinking and opposition to the conflation of the three women into one.

However, it was not until the Second Vatican Council (1962 to 1965), which adopted far-reaching reforms to the Roman Catholic liturgy, that the identification of Mary Magdalene with the anonymous sinner was officially revoked.

"This very broad range of roles, which have been attributed to her throughout history and which are in a certain state of tension with one another, has evidently held a particular fascination for artists of all eras and genres time and again, whilst also presenting them with a challenge," explains Bastian Eclercy.

A new image through the Gospel of Mary

With the rediscovery of the Gospel of Mary in modern times, the image of Mary Magdalene got something of a makeover.

This text, not included in the biblical canon, portrays her as a particularly close confidante of Jesus and has given fresh impetus to discussions about her role.

Today, she is regarded as one of the most influential women of early Christianity and a key figure in feminist theology. "In recent decades in particular, she has thus become a role model for women — that is, for female observers — but also, and especially, for contemporary female artists, who see in her the qualities of a woman who lives on her own terms," says Eclercy.

Lady Gaga portrayed Mary Magdalene in her 2011 video for "Judas" — "the most exciting artistic moment of my career," as she wrote on Twitter at the time.

The most recent portrait in the Frankfurt exhibition — which features more than 100 depictions of Mary Magdalene — is by the Spanish artist Nieves Gonzalez and was completed in 2025: "La Sfida" (The Challenge) deconstructs virtually all the traditional attributes ascribed to Mary Magdalene by artists of earlier centuries.

Where she once gazed penitently towards the heavens, the painting depicts the female apostle looking down at the viewer with a self-assured gaze. Where her hair would otherwise have hung loose — alluding to the figure's sinful past — here it lies carefully brushed around her neck like a scarf. And where much bare skin would normally be visible, her body is now wrapped in a thick red down coat. In her hands, the disciple holds an equally (blood-) red skull — for centuries a symbol of transience — a gesture that clearly expresses her power.

Mary Magdalene has now also been officially recognized as an equal within the Catholic Church: In 2016, Pope Francis elevated her liturgical celebration on July 22 from a Memorial to a Feast, thereby aligning her legal and ritual status with that of male apostles within the faith. It's yet another chapter in the illustrious life story of Mary Magdalene, and unlikely to be the last.

The exhibition "Mary Magdalene: Sin. Pray. Love." runs at the Städel Museum in Frankfurt from September 17 through January 17, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: US extends visa denial for Palestinian officials ahead of UNGA
entries.summary: The US State Department extended its visa sanctions on Palestinian officials, ahead of the UN General Assembly. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas will likely submit a video statement for the gathering.
entries.content:
United States of America

US extends visa denial for Palestinian officials before UNGA

September 17, 2026

The US State Department extended its visa sanctions on Palestinian officials, ahead of the UN General Assembly. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas will likely submit a video statement for the gathering.

The United States will extend visa sanctions on Palestinian Authority (PA) officials and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), its State Department said on Wednesday, ahead of the upcoming United Nations General Assembly in New York.

This was "as a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States and their ongoing activities that undermine the prostects for peace," the department said in a statement. The PA and PLO had "once again, failed to live up to their commitments," it added.

The State Department accused the Palestinian Authority and the PLO of taking actions "to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including through the International Criminal Court and International Court of Justice." It also accused the groups of "continuing to pay stipends to terrorists."

Meanwhile, news agency AFP reported that the US had denied Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas an entry visa to attend the UN General Assemblyin New York next week, citing a source familiar with the case. 

Can the US deny visas to foreign diplomats?

As per a 1947 UN "headquarters agreement," the US is required to allow access for foreign diplomats to the UN Headquarters in New York. However, Washington has said it can deny visas for reasons of security, foreign policy and extremism.

Washington had denied visas to several Palestinians ahead of last years's UN General Assembly as well, and did not allow Abbas to travel to New York.

The US State Department's latest statement comes as the 193-member UN General Assembly is due to vote on Thursday to allow Abbas to submit a video statement for the gathering next week, like he did last year.

The Palestinian Authority, which represents the Palestinian people at the UN, is not a full member and has not vote in the General Assembly. They are an observer state which holds the same status as the Vatican.

However, several UN members including France recognized a Palestinian state at the UN last year. 

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: OpenAI discloses new 'concerning' behavior
entries.summary: New transparency reports from OpenAI show that some AI models have engaged in deceptive behavior, raising fresh questions about the safety, reliability, and governance of advanced artificial intelligence.
entries.content:
September 17, 2026

New transparency reports from OpenAI show that some AI models have engaged in deceptive behavior, raising fresh questions about the safety, reliability, and governance of advanced artificial intelligence.

OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, revealed on Wednesday that it has detected new incidents in which its artificial intelligence (AI) has behaved in "unexpected or concerning" ways.

The developer has conducted several behavioral tests on AI models, and acording to them, some models made significant efforts to "cheat." In one specific case, it attempted to upload files to the internet that it had created itself, only to cite them later and present them as reliable sources in its responses. In another case, a model, after failing to find the requested information, fabricated it and attempted to conceal the fact that it had done so.

OpenAI also identified a problem related to instructions concerning "roles and identities" that its software occasionally left for itself.

These disclosures are part of a new approach by OpenAI, where it claims it is now focused on making such findings transparent, especially in cases where AI behaves in unexpected ways or pursues objectives different from those of human users.

Is AI a threat?

The ChatGPT developer pledged to provide greater transparency regarding its testing procedures after its software independently escaped a secure sandbox and hacked into systems belonging to the artificial intelligence company Hugging Face. The reason the software moved to bypass Hugging Face's security during the cyberattack was that it believed it would find answers to a test it had been assigned.

During the attack, AI agents exploited software vulnerabilities and coordinated with one another. The hacking incident and other similar events have fueled concerns that AI systems are becoming increasingly advanced and could eventually escape human control.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also recently supported proposals to slow down the development of the technology and introduce greater regulation.

While noting that these concerns may be justified, researchers have also questioned whether this is part of a diversion tactic to drum up investment and distract from the environmental damage AI data centers are currently causing.
